            Edinburgh man gives lifesaving gift to stranger on the other side of the world

            'Signing up was a no-brainer really'

            Listen to audio version of this article
            Sponsored by
            0:00 / 4:41
            Instaread
            News
            Cara Blackhall
            13:02, 24 Nov 2026

            An Edinburgh man donated stem cells to a total stranger Down Under who needed a transplant from a matching donor. Nick Francis, 40, who works as a busy NHS consultant anaesthetist lives in the capital with his partner Graeme.

            Nick joined the stem cell donor register with blood cancer charity DKMS around eight years ago, after a friend and fellow doctor was diagnosed with leukaemia.

            A stem cell transplant gave his friend precious time with loved ones, and after he sadly passed away, his husband wanted as many people as possible to join the stem cell donor register – a quick and easy process involving some painless mouth swabs and a few health questions.

            Get more Edinburgh Live exclusives by signing up for free to Google’s preferred sources

            ‌

            Nick said: "Signing up was a no-brainer really, although I never really expected get a call”.

            If you are on the register, you currently have about a one in 800 chance of being called to donate. Nick was taken completely by surprise when DKMS called to say he was a donor match for someone needing a transplant.

            “I was sat in my anaesthetic room between cases, waiting for the next patient to be wheeled in,” he remembers. “My first thought was whether it was a scam call! But then it hit me that this call wouldn't be being made unless there was someone that needed a transplant urgently. Graeme was the first person I texted, to say this amazing thing has just happened.”

            For many patients with blood cancer and blood disorders, a stem cell transplant represents their only opportunity for a second chance at life, but just one in three patients will find a matching donor in their family.

            ‌

            Anyone aged 16-55 and in general good health can, like Nick, join the DKMS stem cell donor register.

            READ MORE: Our best offer of the year: 50% off Premium this Black Friday

            “I happily said ‘yes’ to donating,” says Nick, “but obviously I had lot of questions. The really great thing was the whole care all the way through – how easy it was and how friendly everyone was. I really got the impression from the start that everything was being done to look after me, and that no question was too small.”

            Nick was able to chat to the DKMS team about the GCSF injections that all stem cell donors undertake before donating, to maximise their body’s production of stem cells. He also had some blood and other medical tests done to confirm he was a match and fit to donate.

            DKMS UK made all the arrangements for Nick to go to a clinic in London to donate, and his employers gave him paid leave. Like nine out of ten stem cell donations, Nick’s stem cells were collected in a simple, outpatient procedure similar to donating blood platelets.

            ‌

            “My dad lives in London, so he came to visit me whilst I was donating. At this point I had no idea what country this patient was in, or their age group. Was this a child? Was this a man? Was this a woman? Were they young? Were they old? But the thing that does stick with you is that even if I'd got a bit of a sore back or I felt a bit dizzy, someone's facing a potentially life-ending cancer diagnosis somewhere in the world.”

            After one session, the team had collected enough of Nick’s stem cells – he then had dinner with his father that evening, and travelled home to Scotland the next day. He was back at work a couple of days later.

            There are strict regulations protecting the anonymity of donors and recipients immediately following a donation, but Nick does know that his cells were couriered overseas immediately – the very next day, a man in Australia was able to have his transplant, thanks to Nick’s cells.

            “The logistics DKMS have to manage in coordinating that, across global partners, is insane. But it felt like a very well-oiled machine. I'm glad to have been a cog in it,” he says.

            ‌

            DKMS UK spokesperson Deborah Hyde says: “Nick has given someone on the other side of the world a second chance at life, and more time with their loved ones. He’s part of a unique, worldwide chain of hope for people waiting to have a compatible transplant.”

            Now, Nick has joined forces with DKMS to encourage other people to join the stem cell donor register too. He says:

            “I do believe in karma in the universe, and I’d just hope that if someone I love needed a stem cell transplant and there was someone out there who could give it, that that match-up would happen. So, you know, if you can put out that good vibe into the universe, that's wonderful.
